But this subplot does something really important for the novel. It exposes the utter fragility of Victorian psychological science. How so?
Well, think about it. Dr. Seard is observing Renfield every day. He is analyzing him, writing extensive notes in his diary, classifying his mania, but he

completely misses the actual supernatural threat exploiting his patient right under his nose. Seart thinks he is studying madness, but he is actually observing the localized effects of an ancient predator.
Precisely. The scientific method fails here because it refuses to account for the irrational.
Seward is so locked into his medical paradigm that he can't see the monster standing outside the window.
